messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 34
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Chaplain
- Trauma Type: Mugging or robbery
- Pcl5: 77

**Clinical Vignette: Patient T.**

T. is a 34-year-old widowed South Eastern Asian man who works as a chaplain at a large urban hospital. He has attended six sessions, and over that time he has slowly begun to share the story that brought him here.

The mugging happened on a damp Tuesday night last October. T. had just finished an evening prayer service in the hospital chapel and was walking to his car in the staff parking lot. He remembers pulling his phone out to check a message from his sister. A man came up fast from behind, pressed something hard into his ribs — T. still isn’t sure if it was a knife or a gun — and demanded his wallet, his phone, his watch. T. froze. He handed everything over without a word. The man shoved him to the ground, and as T. fell, his head hit the concrete curb. He lay there for what felt like minutes, blood seeping from a cut above his eye, waiting for the man to come back and finish him. No one came. Eventually he stumbled up and called security from a payphone.

In the weeks after, T. couldn’t stop replaying the moment of the shove. The feel of wet asphalt against his cheek. The smell of exhaust and garbage. The sound of footsteps running away. He began avoiding the parking lot, taking long detours through the emergency room entrance, then switching to a ride-share service. That worked for a while, but last month he found himself unable to enter the hospital at all. He started calling in sick, then using vacation days. Three weeks ago he took a leave of absence. His supervisor, a kind older priest, has called twice. T. lets the calls go to voicemail.

His work as a chaplain used to give him purpose — sitting with families in the ICU, holding space for grief, offering a quiet presence when words failed. Now he feels like a fraud. He tells me: “I’m supposed to be the one who stays calm when everything falls apart. But I can’t even walk to my own car.” The thought of standing beside a trauma patient, of hearing fear in someone’s voice, makes his chest tighten. He stopped visiting the emergency room months ago. He says he feels hollow, like the mugging emptied something inside him that used to be full.

At home, T. lives alone in a small apartment that used to feel safe. His wife died of cancer three years ago, and for a long time the apartment was a sanctuary. Now he sleeps on the living room couch, facing the door, a chair wedged under the knob. He keeps a baseball bat next to the couch. He doesn’t sleep well — maybe three or four hours a night. His dreams are violent, vivid replays of the mugging, but sometimes the man has his wife’s face, or the dream ends with T. lying dead on the asphalt while a nurse he knows walks past without seeing him. He wakes drenched in sweat, heart pounding, and it takes him an hour to convince himself he’s not still there.

He avoids crowds. He avoids the dark. He checks his rearview mirror constantly when driving, even in broad daylight. The other day a stranger brushed past him in a grocery store aisle and he dropped his basket, spun around, fists raised. The stranger apologized. T. stood there shaking for ten minutes. He hasn’t been back to that store.

He tells me he feels ashamed most of the time — ashamed that he didn’t fight back, ashamed that he can’t “just get over it,” ashamed that he, a chaplain, a man who has sat with dying children and grieving parents, is undone by a single act of violence that lasted sixty seconds. He doesn’t pray anymore. He says he’s not angry at God; he just doesn’t know what to say. The silence feels safer.

In session, he is soft-spoken, his hands folded in his lap. He checks the door before he sits down. We are building trust slowly. He still carries the scar above his right eyebrow, a small white line. He touches it sometimes when he talks about that night. He is trying. He is here. But he is still lying on that curb, waiting for someone to come back.
